docs.title: VALORADA Documentation
docs.text: Welcome to the VALORADA project GitHub documentation.

docs.title: About the Project
docs.text:
VALORADA (Validated Local Risk Actionable Data for Adaptation) is a Horizon Europe project (Grant Agreement No. 101112837) whose goal is to empower European regions and cities to steer societal transformation toward sustainable, climate‑resilient development. It aligns with the EU Adaptation Mission supporting 150 regions to become climate‑resilient by 2030 through: * Accelerating societal transformations * Demonstrating systemic adaptation pathways * Improving access to and usability of climate data

The project reveals and enhances the “climate value” of locally collected socio‑economic, demographic and land‑use data by integrating it into risk understanding, adaptation planning and decision support. Practical instruments include Climate Impact Chains, an Indicator & Dataset Catalog (Excel + dashboard), a Climate‑data Valuation Framework, and visualisation examples.

Further information: Project website • Demonstrators • EU Adaptation Mission

This site contains documentation about:

  1. Climate Impact Chains (CICs) co-developed with stakeholders in demonstrator regions.
  2. The Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) European Climate Data Explorer (ECDE) application and related datasets.
  3. The VALORADA Climate-data Valuation Framework used to assess the value of datasets for climate risk reduction. You can download it here.
  4. Indicator & Dataset Catalog: linked Excel view, static dashboard, and source repositories connecting indicators to CIC narratives and valuation criteria.

Use the left navigation to explore each section. A quick overview:

docs.title: 🧬 Climate Impact Chains
docs.text: Cause–effect sequences linking climate hazards (heat, drought, wildfire, flood, etc.) to socio-economic and ecological impacts. Each chain page includes: * Main risk statement * Key policy issues * Sequential impact diagrams (with descriptive alternatives) * Narrative explaining mechanisms

docs.title: 📊 Data & Tools

docs.title: 🗂 Indicator & Dataset Catalog
docs.text:
VALORADA provides a catalogue of climate adaptation–relevant indicators and datasets, linking to Climate Impact Chains, valuation criteria, and dashboard visualisations. The content is rendered in different views:

  • A user‑friendly Excel table created by linking all data together. Download directly: catalog.xlsx
  • A static dashboard deployment: Static dashboard
  • Repository sources for further exploration: catalog repository and dashboard repository

These resources connect underlying indicators to the CIC narratives and the valuation framework criteria.

Project repository: documentation repository

docs.title: Climate Impact Chains (CICs)
docs.text:
Climate Impact Chains describe the relationship between a climate hazard and its cascading impacts across ecological, social, infrastructural and economic components of a system. They help identify indirect impacts, risks of maladaptation, feedback loops, and leverage points for intervention.

The CICs in VALORADA were co-developed with stakeholders in demonstrator regions to ensure practical relevance.

docs.title: Available Chains
docs.text: Chain Main Risk Hazards Urban Ecosystems Degradation of urban ecosystems due to heat & drought High temperature, drought Heat & Health in Transport Heat affecting people’s health & mobility systems High temperature Drought & Agriculture Drought affecting agricultural production & rural livelihoods Drought, heat Wildfire Drought & heat increasing wildfire risk High temperature, drought Floods & Rural Livelihoods Floods affecting rural livelihoods Extreme precipitation

docs.title: How to Read a Chain
docs.text: Each chain page includes: 1. Main risk statement (problem framing) 2. Key policy issues (action-relevant concerns) 3. Sequential impact diagrams with explanatory text 4. Narrative sequences describing causal pathways

docs.title: Using CICs for Policy & Planning
docs.text:
• Identify leverage points (e.g. maintenance capacity, ecosystem health, data availability)
  • Expose compound risks (e.g. drought + heat → wildfire + ecosystem degradation)
  • Inform adaptation strategies (early warning, resilient infrastructure, water governance)
  • Support stakeholder dialogue around cascading effects

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
Future iterations may include scoring of sequence severity, overlay of adaptation options, and links to relevant indicators in the ECDE application.

Proceed to an individual chain using the navigation.

docs.title: CIC 1 – Urban Ecosystems Degradation (Heat & Drought)
docs.text: Main Risk: Degradation of urban ecosystems due to urban heat and droughts.

docs.title: Key Policy Issues
docs.text:
• Urban heat island effect and drought degrading urban green spaces.
  • Loss of ecosystem services (temperature control, recreation areas).
  • Introduction of foreign pests and shifts in plant–disease patterns.
  • Stress on aquatic life and species distribution changes.
  • Need for resilient urban planning, green infrastructure, ecosystem monitoring.
  • Address social vulnerability (elderly, health‑compromised groups).

docs.title: 1. Institutional impacts
docs.text: Reduced maintenance & inspection capacity accelerates degradation.

docs.title: 2. Expansion of pests and pathogens
docs.text: Heat & drought enable spread and persistence.

docs.title: 3. Drought & heat on river ecosystems
docs.text: Aquatic habitat degradation under compounded stress.

docs.title: 4. Heat on pests & tree degradation
docs.text: Tree health declines; new pest assemblages emerge.

docs.title: 5. Promotion of invasive species
docs.text: Specialised species decline; invasive species fill niches.

docs.title: 6. Population dynamics & forage availability
docs.text: Extreme heat alters growth, reproduction, food webs.

docs.title: 7. Plant physiology
docs.text: Stress in photosynthesis, respiration, water regulation reduces resilience.

docs.title: 8. Heat & air pollution
docs.text:
Higher temperatures exacerbate pollutant formation impacting vegetation.

Return to Overview.

docs.title: CIC 2 – Heat & Health in Mobility Systems
docs.text: Main Risk: Heat affecting people’s health in urban transport contexts and degrading social & environmental determinants of health.

docs.title: Key Policy Issues
docs.text:
• Heat stress & accidents (public transport, cycling, walking).
  • Overheating infrastructure (roads, vehicles).
  • Vulnerable groups (elderly, children, pre-existing conditions).
  • Need for early warning & public health interventions.
  • Resilient transport & cooling spaces.

docs.title: 10. Increased water- & food-borne disease
docs.text: Return to Overview.

docs.title: CIC 3 – Drought & Agricultural Livelihoods
docs.text: Main Risk: Drought affecting agricultural production and rural livelihoods.

docs.title: Key Policy Issues
docs.text:
• Water scarcity & competing uses.
  • Soil erosion, salinisation & land degradation.
  • Declining productivity & livelihood vulnerability.
  • Need for sustainable water management & ecosystem restoration.

docs.title: 2. High temperature + evapotranspiration → agricultural drought & soil erosion
3. Drought types → water restriction & fodder shortage
5. Hydrological drought → aquatic ecosystem imbalance

docs.title: CIC 4 – Wildfire Risk Escalation
docs.text: Main Risk: Drought and heat increasing the risk of wildfire.

docs.title: Key Policy Issues
docs.text:
• Elevated wildfire risk (heat, drought, poor forest management).
  • Fuel load from storms & lack of maintenance.
  • Tourism pressure increasing ignition & exposure.
  • Need for integrated forest & wildfire management.

docs.title: 7. Socio-economic & ecological impacts

docs.title: CIC 5 – Floods & Rural Livelihoods
docs.text: Main Risk: Floods affecting rural livelihoods.

docs.title: Key Policy Issues
docs.text:
• Flooding of agricultural land & rural infrastructure.
  • Risk of dam failure & chemical contamination.
  • Outmigration & governance erosion increasing multi-hazard risks.
  • Need for robust flood management & rural development policies.

docs.title: VALORADA Climate-data Valuation Framework
docs.text:
Putting a value on data is challenging for two main reasons: 1. The value of data depends on the context in which it’s used. 2. No single measure can make data value completely objective.

Valuation methods can still help estimate usefulness and make value more comparable across contexts. Methods may be quantitative or qualitative, and subjective (judgement-based) or objective (evidence-based).

The VALORADA Climate-data Valuation Framework helps decision‑makers understand and reach consensus on the importance of existing data for reducing climate risks. It provides a structured mental map using measures highlighted by climate adaptation experts.

The goal isn’t to impose a fixed standard, but to foster informed discussion about how valuable data and information are for tackling climate challenges.

You can download the Valuaiton Framework here.

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
Four Value Dimensions: * Relevance (contribution to knowledge generation) * Strategic Value (alignment with policy agendas) * Usability (resource efficiency & integration ease) * Quality (provenance, accuracy, completeness)

Twelve Criteria (3 per dimension): Each criterion defines an attribute of a dataset; definitions clarify rationale and scope to ensure consistent interpretation.

docs.title: Relevance
docs.text:
1. Climate Risk Understanding
  2. Irreplaceability
  3. Performance (versatility across indicators)

docs.title: Strategic Value
docs.text:
1. Decision‑making Capacity
  2. Municipal Policy Alignment
  3. Multi‑level Policy Connection

docs.title: Usability
docs.text:
1. Resource Efficiency
  2. Fit with Existing Structures
  3. Maintenance Requirements

docs.title: Quality
docs.text:
1. Provenance
  2. Precision & Accuracy
  3. Completeness

docs.title: Relevance 1 – Climate Risk Understanding
docs.text: Assesses contribution to understanding vulnerabilities, exposure, impacts, adaptive capacity. Indicators include: identification, quantification, socio‑economic & geospatial detail, temporal/spatial suitability, monitoring continuity. Scoring: High (5–4), Moderate (3–2), Low (1–0).

docs.title: Relevance 2 – Irreplaceability
docs.text: Evaluates uniqueness and non‑substitutability (granularity, historical continuity, region specificity). Scoring: High, Moderate, Low.

docs.title: Relevance 3 – Performance Value
docs.text: Versatility across multiple risk indicators, compound risk support, multi‑scale applicability, integrability.

docs.title: Strategic Value 1 – Decision‑making Capacity
docs.text: Directly informs prioritisation, planning, monitoring of adaptation/mitigation.

docs.title: Strategic Value 2 – Municipal Policy Alignment
docs.text: Supports climate action plans, infrastructure management, cross‑sector coordination, regulatory compliance.

docs.title: Strategic Value 3 – Multi‑level Policy Connection
docs.text: Aligns with regional/national frameworks; aids reporting and governance coordination.

docs.title: Usability 1 – Resource Efficiency
docs.text: Ease of use without major new tools, funding or expertise; accessible formats; minimal training.

docs.title: Usability 2 – Fit with Existing Structures
docs.text: Compatibility with mandates, workflows, legal/data governance; low integration friction.

docs.title: Usability 3 – Maintenance Requirements
docs.text: Effort, cost, update frequency, automation potential, stability of sources.

docs.title: Quality 1 – Provenance
docs.text: Transparency of origin, collection, curation, metadata quality, standards compliance.

docs.title: Quality 2 – Precision & Accuracy
docs.text: Granularity, correctness, validation, bias absence, coverage of key variables.

docs.title: Quality 3 – Completeness
docs.text: Inclusion of necessary variables, temporal continuity, spatial coverage, internal consistency.

docs.title: Scoring Guidance (0–5)
docs.text: Range Interpretation 5–4 High – strong support for climate risk reduction 3–2 Moderate – useful with limitations 1–0 Low – limited reliability/applicability

docs.title: Suggested Evaluation Steps
docs.text:
1. Define decision context.
  2. List candidate datasets.
  3. Score each criterion (evidence + judgement).
  4. Record rationale & uncertainty.
  5. Aggregate (equal weights unless justified otherwise).
  6. Prioritise for integration or investment.

Return to Home.

docs.title: European Climate Data Explorer (ECDE) – Indicator Visualisation Application
docs.text:
The European Climate Data Explorer (ECDE) indicator visualisation application (referred to as the ECDE application) is a web application of the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S). It allows flexible temporal and spatial exploration and analysis of recent past trends and projected future changes for a range of key climate indicators from multiple datasets.

Application: https://apps.copernicus-climate.eu/c3s-apps/ecde/

docs.title: Purpose & Development
docs.text: The development of the ECDE application was driven by the European Environment Agency (EEA) to address information needs regarding climate impact indicators relevant to national climate change adaptation initiatives across the EU. The list of indicators is based on a technical report from the European Topic Centre on Climate Change Impacts, Vulnerability and Adaptation (ETC‑CCA).

docs.title: Indicator Scope
docs.text: The indicators describe how climate variability and change of essential climate variables can impact sectors such as health, agriculture, forestry, energy, tourism, and water/coastal management. They have been used in VALORADA during the implementation of climate dashboards.

docs.title: Data Access & Documentation
docs.text:
• Catalogue entry (indicator data): https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/datasets/sis-ecde-climate-indicators?tab=overview
  • Underpinning data description: https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/CKB/Input+data+underpinning+the+European+Climate+Data+Explorer%3A+Description+of+the+datasets+and+variables
  • Sources: ERA5 reanalysis and an ensemble of downscaled Euro‑Cordex projections (full time series for individual models).

docs.title: Emerging User Requirements (VALORADA)
docs.text:
Through VALORADA, requirements emerged to assist non‑expert users with aggregated products for regional and local climate risk assessment using C3S data. To support intermediate users, C3S will publish a new dataset providing: * Multi‑model statistics * Pre‑calculated reference periods and anomalies * Climatologies and ensemble statistics

These will be derived from the Climate indicators for Europe from 1940 to 2100 dataset—the same dataset that underpins the interactive ECDE application.

Return to Home.

docs.title: VALORADA Demonstrator Platforms
docs.text: The VALORADA platforms provide tools to analyse territorial risks across various themes - such as agriculture, forest, flooding, urban vegetation, urban climatology, and more—through interactive visualisation of indicators. These thematic insights are complemented by climate indicators, enabling users to explore vulnerabilities and support local adaptation strategies.
